title: Rescuing the trapped from the rubble near the US embassy in Nairobi

trailer.text: The rescue unit of Israel's Home Front Command, whose members train on simulated disaster sites, was sent to Nairobi in 1998 after the bombing at the US embassy.

A few hours after the bombings at the US embassies in Kenya and Tanzania, First Sgt. Ilan Cryton received the call, and according to JTA, by Saturday morning he and 150 other Israeli soldiers, physicians and rescue specialists were already in Nairobi.
According to CBS News, Israel was among the first to arrive to help.

Israeli sniffer dogs discovered a Kenyan man alive under the rubble, and according to JTA, after several hours of digging the Israelis brought out Sammy Nganga from Gateway House, the building next to the embassy.
According to CBS News, on Sunday an Israeli team also rescued a mother and her son from an upper floor of a 22-story building near the embassy.

paragraphs.text: According to the US State Department, on August 7, 1998, at 10:30, truck bombs exploded at the US embassies in Kenya and Tanzania.

According to the State Department, at the embassy in Nairobi approximately 212 people were killed and approximately 4,000 wounded, and at the embassy in Dar es Salaam 11 were killed and more than 85 wounded.
According to the State Department, because of the destruction and confusion, local first responders were not able to reach the site in Nairobi immediately.
According to CBS News, a group called the "Islamic Army for the Liberation of Holy Places" claimed responsibility for the attacks, and Israeli intelligence agents were not familiar with it.
In November 1998, the United States indicted Osama bin Laden and 21 other members of al-Qaeda for the bombings and for conspiring to commit other acts of terrorism.
Kenya cut diplomatic relations with Israel after the 1973 Yom Kippur War, as did most African states.
But the economic links between the two countries remained close.
Hundreds of Israeli specialists worked in Kenya on industrial and agricultural projects.
In July 1976, after the rescue of the hostages at Entebbe, Kenya secretly allowed Israeli transport planes to refuel in Nairobi.
According to the Jewish Journal, senior Defense Ministry officials in Tel Aviv described the Nairobi mission as a debt of honor.
On Friday afternoon, a few hours after the bombings, First Sgt. Ilan Cryton received the call he had been expecting.
He said he had two hours to get ready, and that luckily he lived close to the base.
According to JTA, by Saturday morning Cryton and 150 other Israeli soldiers, physicians and rescue and trauma specialists had arrived in Nairobi, and they rushed to the bomb site.
According to the Jewish Journal, most of the team members were reservists.
Ehud Barak, who at the time the article was written was leader of the opposition for Labor, commanded the backup group in Nairobi in July 1976, during the Entebbe operation.
According to CBS News, Israel was among the first to arrive to help, and was geographically the closest American ally able to assist.
The Israelis worked with equipment they had brought from Israel, and sometimes with their bare hands, alongside Kenyan soldiers.
They used a 150-foot crane, drills and blowtorches.
Cryton said that he and a small team climbed the emergency stairs of a building whose interior had been completely destroyed.

According to the Jewish Journal, during the rescue of the Kenyan survivor, the commander of Gil Weiner's team insisted that they work only from the side and above, for fear that haste would bring tons of rubble down on the trapped man and the rescuers.
According to the Jewish Journal, the team members expected to bring out more dead than alive.
According to CBS News, 64 specialists from the Fairfax County Fire Department in Virginia were also brought to Nairobi.
Israeli sniffer dogs, wearing cloth tags with a Star of David, discovered a Kenyan man alive under the rubble.
According to JTA, after several hours of digging the Israelis brought out Sammy Nganga from a ground-floor office of Gateway House, the building next to the embassy.
In the Jewish Journal his name was written Sammy Ngana.
It was the soldier Gil Wiener who dragged out the first survivor rescued by the Israeli dog squad.
Wiener and his team talked with the survivor for six hours, until they got him out of the steel-and-concrete trap.
The pain was so severe that the survivor begged the Israelis to let him die.
Lt. Nahum Nesher, a doctor on the team, told him that he would not let him die.

stations.title: A mother and her son, and also the dead

paragraphs.text: According to CBS News, on Sunday an Israeli search team rescued a mother and her son from an upper floor of a 22-story building near the embassy.
According to CBS News, the Israelis also pulled from the rubble the bodies of Kenyan victims of a bomb aimed at Americans.
Cryton said that he sees flashes of bodies and body parts, but that he is also proud of his unit.
When the crowd in Nairobi praised Gil Wiener on Saturday night, he protested and said he was not a hero.
According to CBS News, when the team returned to Tel Aviv on August 13, Prime Minister Netanyahu said that a bond between victims had now been formed.
"We're fighting a common battle against international terrorism", Netanyahu said.
JTA reported, in an undated article, that Israel is helping Kenya build a disaster response center.
According to JTA, Israel's ambassador to Kenya, Emmanuel Seri, announced this in Nairobi.
In 2006 the Jerusalem Post noted that in 1998 Israel had sent a team from the Home Front Command's rescue unit to Nairobi.
Gil Wiener was 29, an architecture student who worked as a lifeguard at the Hebrew University swimming pool in Jerusalem to pay for his studies.
According to the Jewish Journal, the unit's members are recruited from all branches of the army in the last year of their three-year regular service, and train at simulated disaster sites.
According to JTA, the unit has 400 engineers, medical personnel and disaster relief experts.
According to JTA, the unit was established in 1982, after the bombing of the IDF headquarters in Tyre during the Lebanon War.
According to the Jewish Journal, the explosion that demolished an army administrative block in the port city of Tyre in 1982 killed 89 soldiers and security service personnel.
According to JTA, the unit gained much of its experience in the 1991 Gulf War, when Iraqi Scud missiles hit population centers in Israel.
The unit also operated abroad: in Buenos Aires after the bombing of the Israeli embassy, and in Mexico and Armenia after earthquakes.
According to JTA, in June 1994 the IDF flew a medical team of doctors and medical staff with medical supplies, food and clothing to Rwanda, to help refugees caught up in a civil war.

According to the Jewish Journal, the unit has served at home and on humanitarian missions on three continents, and some of the team members in Nairobi were veterans of the operations in Buenos Aires and Armenia.
